Read _docs/BACKEND.md section 13 'Compliance: GDPR / nFADP erasure & data-subject rights' in full (the only substantive privacy writeup in the repo), _rules/STRUCTURAL_RULES.md Pattern D, _rules/DB_SCHEMA.md line 19, and _plans/OPS_RUNBOOK.md's 'Data retention' and 'Backups' sections. Read the actual code, not just the docs describing it: app/api/profile/export/route.ts (full), app/api/cron/process-deletions/route.ts (full TABLES_CLEARED array + comments), app/api/profile/delete/route.ts and request-deletion/route.ts (via BACKEND.md's citations, cross-checked), lib/gdpr/anonymize-guest.ts, supabase/migrations/20260602083300_financial_retention_on_delete.sql, supabase/migrations/20260713150000_gdpr_deletion_completeness.sql, supabase/migrations/040_client_notes.sql, and the four dashboard-notes migrations (20260328_coiffeur_dashboard.sql, 20260328_waxing_dashboard.sql, 20260328_spa_dashboard.sql, 20260329_makeup_dashboard.sql) to check FK cascade behavior on client_id/customer_id columns. Read the full live privacy policy at app/[locale]/privacy/components/PrivacyContent.tsx (194 lines). Read app/[locale]/_components/primitives/CookieConsent.tsx, app/api/me/consent/route.ts, lib/posthog-server.ts, and components-legacy/PostHogProvider.tsx to verify the consent mechanism actually gates capture. Parsed _inventory/_db-snapshot.json (146 tables, rls flags) and _inventory/_db-columns.json (per-table column lists) with a Python regex sweep for PII-shaped column names, producing a list of 69 tables and ~147 matching columns, manually reviewed to separate real personal/sensitive data from false positives (product/service 'name' columns, generic 'photo_type' enums, etc.). Ran greps for privacy/gdpr/nfadp/dsgvo/datenschutz across _backend-system, _docs, _rules, _design-system, CLAUDE.md, and both hook directories; for cookie/consent/marketing-pixel strings across app/lib/components; for 'processing register'/'RoPA'/'Art. 30'/'DPA' across the estate; for age/minor/parental-consent handling across app/lib; and for 'breach notif'/'data breach'/'72 hour' across _docs/_rules/_backend-system/_plans. Verified two statutory claims live via WebSearch (nFADP Art. 12(5) register exemption does not apply once sensitive data is processed; GDPR Art. 30(5) small-enterprise exemption excludes Art. 9 special-category processing) and the Schrems II Privacy Shield invalidation date (16 July 2020) plus the EU-US Data Privacy Framework adequacy decision (July 2023), because the live privacy policy cites 'Privacy Shield' by name and that claim needed checking against the real timeline, not memory.

findings.title: Privacy/nFADP/GDPR has zero presence in the backend law taxonomy
findings.principle: Add `privacy-data-protection` as a 16th topic in _backend-system/research/ and audit/, and give it a LAW.md row set once LAW.md exists, on the same terms as the other 15 topics (data-modeling, authn, security, etc). Until that file exists, any session touching a new table with a name-shaped, email-shaped, phone-shaped, note-shaped, or photo-shaped column must treat _docs/BACKEND.md section 13 plus this finding set as the interim source of truth, not training memory.
findings.why: The owner's own stated reason for building _backend-system/ was 'it keeps making stuff up when I open a new session' for backend decisions. That diagnosis applies with full force to privacy: a fresh session adding a new client-facing note field, a new photo upload, or a new consent toggle has nowhere in the law layer to check what Solen already decided, so it will either invent a policy or silently skip the question. The irony is that real, non-trivial privacy engineering already exists (an anonymize-not-delete erasure trigger, a two-path deletion flow, a consent-gated PostHog client, a bilingual privacy policy with a processor table) scattered across _docs/BACKEND.md, four migration files, a React component, and a legal page that none of them reference each other from.
findings.local_evidence: _backend-system/README.md's own topic table lists exactly 15 topics (data-modeling, transactions-concurrency, migrations, backup-recovery, authn, authz, api-design, security, rate-limiting, file-storage, jobs-async, webhooks, caching, observability, reliability) with no privacy/data-protection entry. The only place a privacy decision is documented at law-file depth is _docs/BACKEND.md section 13, which the folder's own README explicitly classifies as DESCRIPTIVE ('how our systems currently work'), not the PRESCRIPTIVE LAW.md layer the rest of the backend gets.
findings.absence_proof: `ls _backend-system/research _backend-system/audit` returns 15 and 8 files respectively, none named privacy/gdpr/data-protection. `grep -ril "privacy\|gdpr\|nfadp\|dsgvo\|datenschutz" _backend-system` hits research/data-modeling.md, backup-recovery.md, rate-limiting.md, observability.md, security.md, and audit/file-storage.md, backup-recovery.md, jobs-async.md, i.e. privacy is mentioned in passing inside six OTHER topics' research, never as its own file.
findings.existing_coverage: partial: _docs/BACKEND.md section 13 (descriptive, ~1400 words, genuinely detailed) plus scattered paragraphs in security.md section 12 (PII encryption) and observability.md (PII-in-logs, cites FADP Art. 24 and GDPR Art. 5(1)(e) once). None of this is dated, frozen law with a tier and a recommended default in the LAW.md sense the other 15 topics get.
findings.where_it_should_live: _backend-system/research/privacy-data-protection.md (new file) + a future LAW.md row; cross-link from _docs/BACKEND.md section 13 rather than duplicating it
findings.enforcement: checklist for now (no LAW.md exists yet for anything); once LAW.md is written, gate:new-pii-column-privacy-check could block a migration that adds a column matching /email|phone|address|note|photo|health|allerg/i to a table without a corresponding line in a to-be-written retention/export/erasure matrix

findings.title: Self-service data export omits every salon-authored client record, including the most sensitive ones
findings.principle: GET /api/profile/export must return every table where a row is keyed to the requesting user as a data subject, not only tables the user themselves wrote to. Before shipping any change to this route, the exported-table list and the erasure `TABLES_CLEARED`/cascade list must be diffed against each other and against a live grep of `client_id UUID.*REFERENCES profiles(id)` / `customer_id UUID.*REFERENCES auth.users(id)`; any table present in one list and absent from the other is a bug, not a design choice, unless a comment names the reason.
findings.why: GDPR Art. 15 (right of access) and Art. 20 (data portability), and nFADP Art. 25 (right to information), entitle a data subject to see personal data an organization holds ABOUT them, not only data they entered themselves. A salon's consultation notes, allergy log, or treatment photos of a client are exactly this: personal data the salon (acting for or alongside Solen) generated about the customer. An export that silently skips these tables makes the self-service access right materially incomplete, which is the specific mechanism a real DSAR complaint would test first.
findings.local_evidence: app/api/profile/export/route.ts:20-142 lists exactly 18 tables via `.eq("user_id", user.id)` calls: profiles, salons (owned), bookings+booking_services, reviews, favorites, user_credits, credit_redemptions, notifications, notification_preferences, user_preferences, loyalty_status, referrals, discovery_saves, discovery_collections, discovery_comments, recurring_booking_rules, push_subscriptions, voucher_redemptions, tips. Cross-referencing the 69-table PII sweep of _inventory/_db-columns.json against this list, at least 13 tables holding first-party client data about the same user are absent from export: client_notes, consultation_notes, client_formulas, nail_client_preferences, hand_chart_notes, barber_cut_history, client_photos, spa_treatment_outcomes, waxing_sensitivity_log, wellness_journals, makeup_face_charts, bridal_workflows, fade_blueprints. All of these DO appear as delete/anonymize targets in app/api/cron/process-deletions/route.ts's TABLES_CLEARED array or cascade via a `client_id ... REFERENCES profiles(id) ON DELETE CASCADE` FK (confirmed by reading the four dashboard-notes migrations directly), so Solen already treats them as the user's personal data for erasure purposes but not for access purposes.
findings.absence_proof: Read app/api/profile/export/route.ts end to end (207 lines); grepped it for each of the 13 table names above, zero matches. Grepped the same 13 names against process-deletions/route.ts and the four migration files, all 13 appear as an erasure or cascade target.
findings.existing_coverage: none: this specific asymmetry between the export list and the erasure list is not named anywhere in _docs/BACKEND.md section 13 (which documents the export endpoint's 18 tables as a fact, not as a gap against the erasure list) or in security.md's Unverified section.
findings.where_it_should_live: app/api/profile/export/route.ts (code fix) + a documented invariant in _backend-system/research/privacy-data-protection.md
findings.enforcement: gate:export-erasure-table-parity, a script that extracts the table-name list from both files and fails CI if either list contains a table the other doesn't, with an explicit allowlist file for intentional one-sided exclusions

findings.title: Special-category personal data is collected with the same consent as ordinary account data
findings.principle: Any column that reveals health status (allergy_notes, skin_sensitivity, medications, skin_condition, pain_level, skin_before/after) or is capable of revealing racial/ethnic origin (disc_skin_tone) must be behind an explicit, separately-recorded consent event distinct from general account creation or ToS acceptance, per GDPR Art. 9(2)(a) and nFADP Art. 6(2)/Art. 5(c). General 'necessary for performance of a contract' (GDPR Art. 6(1)(b)) is NOT a valid basis for Art. 9 special-category data on its own; explicit consent (or a narrow Art. 9(2) exemption Solen would need to name) is required regardless of whether the customer also agreed to book a service.
findings.why: A beauty/wellness booking product legitimately needs to know a client is allergic to a product or has sensitive skin, that's a real safety need, not a design mistake. But collecting it is legally a different, higher-obligation category of processing than 'what's your name and phone number,' and treating it identically means Solen has no record it ever obtained the specific consent this category of data requires, which is the first thing a regulator or a complainant checks.
findings.local_evidence: profiles carries disc_skin_tone, disc_hair_length, disc_hair_texture, hair_condition, hair_type, hair_thickness, hair_beard, date_of_birth (_inventory/_db-columns.json). waxing_sensitivity_log carries reaction_level, affected_zones, medications, sun_exposure_recent (supabase/migrations/20260328_waxing_dashboard.sql:16-28, explicitly commented '-- health-sensitive data' in the migration's own header). nail_client_preferences carries allergy_notes and skin_sensitivity. spa_treatment_outcomes carries skin_before/skin_after. wellness_journals carries pain_level (1-10 CHECK constraint) and skin_condition. None of these tables, nor profiles, has a distinct consent-timestamp column analogous to profiles.analytics_consent (added by migration 20260714230441 specifically to give the cookie-banner's analytics choice a server-side, auditable record); the only consent infrastructure that exists is for marketing/analytics cookies, not for special-category health data.
findings.absence_proof: `grep -rn "special.categor\|Art\. 9\|sensitive.*consent\|health.*consent" app lib _docs _rules` across the estate returns nothing; `grep -n "consent" supabase/migrations/20260328_waxing_dashboard.sql supabase/migrations/20260328_spa_dashboard.sql` returns nothing despite the waxing migration's own comment flagging the table as health-sensitive.
findings.existing_coverage: none: the privacy policy (PrivacyContent.tsx:18) lists 'Allergien/Allergies' as one bullet inside ordinary 'Booking Data' with no distinct legal-basis statement; consultation-notes and skin/health fields elsewhere are not named in the policy at all (see finding 04).
findings.where_it_should_live: a new consent step in the intake/consultation-notes UI flow (wherever consultation_notes/waxing_sensitivity_log/nail_client_preferences rows are first created) + a documented legal-basis table in _backend-system/research/privacy-data-protection.md
findings.enforcement: checklist for now; behavioral rule: no migration adding a health/sensitivity/allergy-shaped column ships without a paired consent-capture column or an explicit documented exemption

findings.title: The live privacy policy is stale against the schema and cites a data-transfer mechanism invalidated six years ago
findings.principle: The privacy policy's processor table (section 4) must name the CURRENT legal transfer mechanism for any non-EU/CH processor, and the policy's data-inventory section (2.1) must be regenerated from the actual schema, not hand-maintained prose, on a fixed cadence (e.g. every migration that touches a table named in the policy, or at minimum quarterly) with the 'last updated' date bumped every time the underlying processing actually changed, not left stale.
findings.why: A privacy policy that names a legal mechanism the CJEU struck down in 2020 doesn't just look outdated, it makes an affirmatively false claim about the legal basis for a real transfer of Swiss/EU customer payment data to a US company (Stripe). A policy whose 'what we collect' section was last true in March 2026 while the schema has since grown to include biometric-adjacent DISC fields and half a dozen clinical-note tables is not protecting Solen legally even though a document EXISTS at the URL; an incomplete privacy notice is treated the same as no notice for the categories it omits.
findings.local_evidence: app/[locale]/privacy/components/PrivacyContent.tsx:59 states Stripe's transfer basis as 'Global (Stripe Privacy Shield)'. The EU-US Privacy Shield was invalidated by the CJEU's Schrems II ruling on 16 July 2020 (verified via WebSearch this run); the current mechanism is the EU-US Data Privacy Framework, adequacy decision July 2023, or Standard Contractual Clauses. PrivacyContent.tsx:134 stamps 'Last updated: 23. März 2026'; profiles.disc_skin_tone/disc_hair_length/disc_hair_texture and the consultation_notes/waxing_sensitivity_log/nail_client_preferences/spa_treatment_outcomes/wellness_journals/makeup_face_charts/bridal_workflows tables (all created by 20260328-20260329 migrations, i.e. BEFORE the policy's own stated last-update date) are never named anywhere in section 2.1's data inventory, which still only says 'Kundennotizen, Präferenzen, Allergien'.
findings.absence_proof: grep of PrivacyContent.tsx for 'disc_' , 'hair_condition', 'skin_tone', 'consultation', 'waxing', 'spa', 'makeup', 'bridal' returns zero matches; grep for 'Privacy Shield' returns one match (section 4 table), grep for 'Data Privacy Framework' or 'Standard Contractual Clauses' returns zero.
findings.existing_coverage: none: this is the ONLY customer-facing legal document in the repo and nothing cross-checks it against the schema
findings.where_it_should_live: app/[locale]/privacy/components/PrivacyContent.tsx (immediate text fix) + a recurring reminder (a comment block at the top of the file naming which migrations require a policy review) since full automation of legal prose is not realistic
findings.enforcement: checklist (a legal-text diff can't be a hard gate) but a lightweight one is feasible: gate:privacy-policy-staleness could warn (not block) when a migration adds a column matching /note|allerg|skin|hair|health|photo/i to a table not already referenced in PrivacyContent.tsx

findings.title: No processing register exists, and the small-business exemption that might otherwise excuse one does not apply
findings.principle: Solen must maintain a Record of Processing Activities (RoPA) naming, per processing purpose: the categories of data subject and data, the legal basis, the recipients/processors, the retention period, and (for special categories) the specific Art. 9/Art. 6(2) basis relied on. The customer-facing processor table in the privacy policy is not a substitute; it omits legal basis and retention-per-category entirely.
findings.why: Both nFADP Art. 12(5) and GDPR Art. 30(5) let organizations under roughly 250 employees skip the formal register, but BOTH carve that exemption back out the moment the organization processes special-category data (verified via WebSearch this run against current legal-guidance sources for both statutes) or the processing is not occasional. Solen's own consultation-notes, waxing-sensitivity, and skin/hair-condition tables (finding 03) put it squarely in the carve-back, not the exemption, regardless of its 28-salon size.
findings.local_evidence: No file anywhere in the repo is titled or structured as a RoPA. PrivacyContent.tsx section 4's processor table has three columns (Provider, Purpose, Region) and no legal-basis or retention column. profiles/waxing_sensitivity_log/nail_client_preferences/spa_treatment_outcomes/wellness_journals (finding 03) constitute non-occasional processing of health-adjacent data, which is the exact trigger both statutes name for losing the small-org exemption.
findings.absence_proof: grep -ril 'processing register|records of processing|RoPA|Art\. 30|Verarbeitungsverzeichnis|processor agreement|data processing agreement' across _docs, _rules, _backend-system returns only unrelated matches (generic uses of 'register'/'DPA' as different acronyms, verified by opening each hit).
findings.existing_coverage: partial: the privacy policy's processor table (PrivacyContent.tsx section 4) covers processors/purpose/region only, none of the RoPA-required fields (legal basis, retention, data subject categories, data categories)
findings.where_it_should_live: a new internal-only doc, e.g. _backend-system/research/privacy-data-protection.md appendix or a standalone _compliance/RoPA.md, NOT the public privacy policy
findings.enforcement: checklist; genuinely not gate-able, this is a document that needs a human legal review, not code

findings.title: Third-party processors and the audit log are outside the erasure cascade, and the codebase already says so
findings.principle: Every processor named in the privacy policy's own table that stores a copy of a user's PII (today: Stripe, PostHog) must have an erasure/anonymization call wired into app/api/cron/process-deletions/route.ts before a deletion run is considered complete for that user, OR the privacy policy must explicitly disclose the exception and its legal basis (e.g. Stripe's own 10-year financial-recordkeeping obligation as a controller in its own right). Additionally, `audit_log.metadata` jsonb payloads that carry a plaintext email (`{ email: user.email }`) must be scrubbed or hashed as part of the same erasure run, not left indefinitely because the FK-level `actor_id SET NULL` gives a false impression of completeness.
findings.why: Anonymize-not-delete only satisfies 'right to erasure' if it actually reaches every place the PII was copied to. A trigger that correctly nulls `bookings.guest_email` while a live Stripe Customer object and a PostHog person profile keep the same email under the same permanent user id is erasure in the primary database only, which is a materially different (and weaker) claim than what the product's own deletion UI implies to the user ('DELETE MY ACCOUNT').
findings.local_evidence: _docs/BACKEND.md section 13's own Gotchas paragraph states this outright: 'Stripe and PostHog are not part of the erasure cascade... This is a real gap against a strict right-to-erasure reading, not just a documentation nuance,' and separately: '`audit_log.metadata` can carry the erased user's email indefinitely... the metadata jsonb payload with the plaintext email is never scrubbed by the trigger, the cron, or any job found in this repo.' Verified live: `grep -rn "stripe.customers.del\|stripe.customers.delete" app lib` (per BACKEND.md's own cited grep) returns nothing; `identifyServerUser` in lib/posthog-server.ts sends the email as a person property with no corresponding delete call in the erasure cron.
findings.absence_proof: Read app/api/cron/process-deletions/route.ts in full (all TABLES_CLEARED entries and both purge helpers, lib/gdpr/purge-client-photo-storage.ts and purge-review-photo-storage.ts, which DO exist for storage bytes); no equivalent purge helper exists for Stripe or PostHog, confirmed by `find . -iname '*purge*' -path '*gdpr*'` returning only the two storage-purge files.
findings.existing_coverage: partial: named explicitly as a known gap inside _docs/BACKEND.md section 13's descriptive prose; never turned into a required behavior with an owner or a deadline
findings.where_it_should_live: app/api/cron/process-deletions/route.ts (add stripe.customers.del + a PostHog person-deletion API call) + lib/gdpr/ (a new purge-processor-pii.ts alongside the two existing storage-purge helpers)
findings.enforcement: gate:erasure-processor-completeness, a checklist item reviewed every time a NEW third-party processor that receives user PII is added (Resend already sends emails with names, worth the same check)

findings.title: No retention schedule exists; three independently-decided numbers stand in for one
findings.principle: Every table holding personal data needs an explicit retention rule, stated as either a fixed duration, an event-triggered deletion (e.g. 'N days after the booking relationship ends'), or 'retained until account deletion, no independent limit,' with the reasoning named. A table with no stated rule defaults to 'retained until account deletion,' never to silent indefinite growth.
findings.why: GDPR Art. 5(1)(e) (storage limitation) and the equivalent nFADP proportionality principle both require that retention be actively justified, not merely 'whatever happens by default.' Right now Solen has three retention numbers that were each decided for a different reason (financial law, a 2026-07-10 OTP-logging sweep, an ad hoc 90-day search-anonymization job) and calls that 'data retention' in its own runbook, while several tables holding real personal or health-adjacent data have never had the question asked.
findings.local_evidence: _plans/OPS_RUNBOOK.md:28-33, the entire 'Data retention (Swiss nFADP notes)' section, is five bullets: search_events (90-day PII null), GDPR account deletion (30-day grace, cites 19-FK, now stale, see finding 02), cron_runs ('grows ~30 rows/day. FOLLOW-UP: add a 90-day purge clause... when it passes ~10k rows' — an explicitly deferred, not-yet-true retention rule), audit_log ('59 rows today... revisit at 50k rows' — same pattern, a size trigger not a time-based retention rule), and an OTP-logging note that is not a retention rule at all. No line addresses: client_notes/consultation_notes/waxing_sensitivity_log/etc after the client relationship with a salon ends, a guest booking that is never converted into an account (guest_bookings, booking_disputes with guest_email), or `profiles.deletion_requested_at` itself if a user changes their mind (does the cancel-during-grace-period path ever clear stale request timestamps left by a since-cancelled request).
findings.absence_proof: grep -n 'retention' across _plans/OPS_RUNBOOK.md, _docs/BACKEND.md, _rules returns only the sections cited above; no retention matrix or per-table schedule file exists anywhere (`find . -iname '*retention*' -not -path './node_modules/*'` returns only OPS_RUNBOOK.md and BACKEND.md, both prose, not a schedule).
findings.existing_coverage: partial: three ad hoc, individually-reasoned rules exist and are documented; a general policy that unifies them does not
findings.where_it_should_live: _backend-system/research/privacy-data-protection.md (a retention table, one row per PII-bearing table) + _plans/OPS_RUNBOOK.md keeps the operational summary
findings.enforcement: checklist now; once a retention doc exists, gate:new-pii-table-retention could require a paired retention-doc entry whenever a migration creates a table with a column matching the PII regex used in this audit

findings.title: No minimum age or minor/guardian-consent policy exists anywhere in the product
findings.principle: Define a minimum onboarding age (GDPR Art. 8 sets the digital-consent floor at 13-16 depending on jurisdiction; Swiss law has no equivalent digital-consent-age provision but general contract-capacity rules mean a minor's booking contract may not bind them without a guardian) and, at minimum, state the age policy in the ToS/privacy policy even before any enforcement is built. Do not validate `profiles.date_of_birth` retroactively into a feature (e.g. age-based service recommendations) without first deciding what the minimum age actually is.
findings.why: A beauty/wellness marketplace plausibly serves minors (a 15-year-old booking a haircut is completely ordinary), and some of the services in scope (waxing, chemical hair treatments, piercings if ever added) carry real safety and consent considerations for minors specifically. Right now the product collects date_of_birth but does nothing with it, which is the exact 'collected but unused, so nobody thought about the actual policy question' shape this whole audit is built to surface.
findings.local_evidence: profiles.date_of_birth exists per _inventory/_db-columns.json. `grep -rn "date_of_birth" app lib` finds the column referenced only in generic profile-update code paths (validation schema, export route), never compared against a minimum-age threshold or used to gate a booking.
findings.absence_proof: grep -rn 'minimum age|min_age|parental consent|guardian|minderjährig|isMinor|under 18|under 16' app lib components (excluding false positives like the literal word 'Package' matching 'age') returns zero real hits after manual review of the raw grep output.
findings.where_it_should_live: signup/onboarding validation (lib/validations.ts) + a stated policy line in the ToS (app/[locale]/terms) and privacy policy
findings.enforcement: checklist; once a policy is decided, a simple Zod refinement on date_of_birth at signup is a gate-able, S-effort fix

findings.title: Whether a salon is a controller, joint controller, or processor for the notes it writes is never decided
findings.principle: For every table where a salon (not Solen) originates the personal data (client_notes, consultation_notes, and the category-specific note/photo tables), name explicitly whether the salon is acting as an independent controller, a joint controller with Solen, or a processor acting on Solen's instructions, because this determines who owes the data subject which right, and whether a controller-to-controller (or joint-controller Art. 26 GDPR / equivalent nFADP) agreement is needed between Solen and each of its 28 salon partners.
findings.why: A controller is defined by who decides the purposes and means of processing, not by who technically holds the database. A salon employee who freely writes 'client has a nut allergy, avoid product X' is deciding, on their own judgment, what to record and why, which is the textbook fact pattern for the salon being an independent controller for that specific note, not merely a data processor executing Solen's instructions. If that's correct, the salon (not just Solen) independently owes that client the GDPR/nFADP data-subject rights for that data, and Solen's platform-wide erasure/export mechanisms are doing the salon's compliance work without an agreement that says so.
findings.local_evidence: supabase/migrations/040_client_notes.sql:19-22 scopes RLS to `s.owner_id = auth.uid()`, i.e. only the specific salon owner who wrote or manages a note can read/write it; Solen's own platform-level admin access is not automatically implied by the RLS policy shown (a service-role/admin client bypasses RLS entirely for the deletion cron, which is a separate, narrower channel than day-to-day salon access). No contract, DPA template, or partner-onboarding document was found addressing this split.
findings.absence_proof: grep -ril 'joint controller|data processing agreement|controller.*processor|Auftragsverarbeit' _docs _rules _backend-system app/[locale]/legal 2>/dev/null returns nothing; `find . -iname '*salon-agreement*' -o -iname '*partner-terms*'` (excluding node_modules) returns nothing.
findings.where_it_should_live: a salon-partner agreement/onboarding doc (does not appear to exist yet at all, in or out of this repo) + a note in _backend-system/research/privacy-data-protection.md naming the controller/processor split per table
findings.enforcement: checklist, this is a legal-drafting question, not a code gate

findings.title: Permanent staff notes about a client are invisible to that client by design, with no stated exemption
findings.principle: A data subject's right of access covers personal data held about them regardless of who wrote it, unless a specific, named exemption applies (e.g. notes that would reveal a third party's data, or genuinely provisional working notes not yet relied upon). If Solen intends to keep permanent staff notes hidden from the client they're about, that decision needs a named legal basis in writing; if no such basis exists, the RLS policy is the wrong shape.
findings.why: Hiding 'permanent' notes from the very customer they describe, while calling the platform-wide export endpoint a 'data export,' sets up exactly the situation a DSAR complaint would surface: a customer requests their data, gets an export that (per finding 02) doesn't include client_notes at all, and separately could never see the 'permanent' half even if it did, because the RLS layer itself partitions note visibility by note_type in a way that structurally excludes the data subject from ever seeing about half of what's recorded about them.
findings.local_evidence: supabase/migrations/040_client_notes.sql:24-26: `CREATE POLICY "client_notes_select_own_booking" ON public.client_notes FOR SELECT USING (customer_id = auth.uid() AND note_type = 'booking')` — this policy exists specifically to show the customer ONLY 'booking'-type notes, never 'permanent'-type notes, and the column comment at the top of the file ('Salon staff can add private notes on clients') frames this as an intentional privacy-from-the-customer design, not an access-rights consideration.
findings.absence_proof: grep -n 'exemption|working note|provisional|Art\. 15' supabase/migrations/040_client_notes.sql and _docs/BACKEND.md returns nothing; no comment anywhere states why 'permanent' notes are access-right-exempt.
findings.where_it_should_live: supabase/migrations (a follow-up migration or documented decision) + the export endpoint (finding 02) once it's decided whether permanent notes should be included
findings.enforcement: checklist; this is a product/legal decision (does the owner WANT clients to see staff notes about them) before it's a code change

findings.title: Breach-notification duty is cited once, buried in an unrelated research file, with no owned procedure
findings.principle: Solen needs a named breach-response procedure: who gets notified internally within what timeframe, what counts as 'high risk' under FADP Art. 24 (Swiss controllers must notify the FDPIC 'as quickly as possible' for a high-risk breach, a materially softer deadline than GDPR's 72 hours but still a real, undischarged duty), and a template for the FDPIC notification and any affected-user notification. This does not need to be elaborate at 28 salons and ~50 profile rows, but it needs to exist BEFORE an incident, not be improvised during one.
findings.why: The single correct citation of FADP Art. 24 already sitting in this codebase is inside observability.md's PII-logging research, framed as a reason to be careful about what goes into logs, not as its own owned procedure. A breach duty that only exists as a side-effect footnote inside an unrelated topic's research file is not a procedure anyone will find under time pressure.
findings.local_evidence: _backend-system/research/observability.md:127 states the FADP Art. 24 obligation in one sentence inside a paragraph about log PII, and nowhere else in the repo does 'breach' co-occur with 'notif' in a procedural context.
findings.absence_proof: grep -ril 'breach notif|data breach|incident response|72 hour' _docs _rules _backend-system _plans returns exactly one file: observability.md, and only in the PII-logging section, confirmed by reading lines 124-135 in full.
findings.existing_coverage: partial: the legal citation is correct and present; the procedure (who, when, how, template) is absent
findings.where_it_should_live: a new short doc, e.g. _plans/OPS_RUNBOOK.md gets an 'Incident response: data breach' section pointing at the legal citation already in observability.md rather than duplicating it
findings.enforcement: checklist; not gate-able (a procedure document, not code)

findings.title: GDPR applies only if Solen actually targets EU data subjects; that determination is never made explicit and the policy currently hedges rather than deciding
findings.principle: State explicitly, once, which regime is primary: Solen is a Swiss sole proprietorship serving (per its own domain and the seeded salon set) Swiss customers, so nFADP is the primary and binding regime under Swiss law regardless of language. GDPR only attaches extraterritorially under Art. 3(2) if Solen actively offers services to, or monitors the behavior of, individuals physically in the EU (e.g. targeted marketing in euros, EU-specific delivery/service availability), not merely because the site is available in French/Italian or a tourist from the EU happens to book a Swiss salon while visiting. Until that determination is made and documented, don't build EU-specific machinery (a full RoPA, an EU representative under Art. 27 GDPR) reflexively, and don't tell users 'you have GDPR rights' if Solen has not concluded GDPR actually applies to them.
findings.why: The current privacy policy already shows the hedge this finding is about: section 7's heading is 'Rechte nach nDSG' but the body says rights exist 'nach dem revidierten Schweizer Datenschutzgesetz (nDSG) sowie ggf. der europäischen DSGVO' (nFADP and, where applicable, GDPR), without ever stating the 'where applicable' test. This is the right instinct (both nDSG rights AND a genuine 'if GDPR applies' qualifier) but leaves the actual determination undone, which risks two opposite failure modes: under-informing an EU customer GDPR really does cover, or over-building EU-specific machinery Solen doesn't yet need at 28 Swiss salons.
findings.local_evidence: app/[locale]/privacy/components/PrivacyContent.tsx:114-117 (section 7 heading and lead sentence) is the only place in the repo that names both regimes together, and it explicitly uses 'ggf.' (German for 'where applicable') without defining the test. The i18n locale set (de/en/fr/it) is itself Swiss-national-language coverage (all four are official Swiss languages), not evidence of EU targeting, contrary to what a session might assume by pattern-matching 'four languages' to 'EU-wide.'
findings.absence_proof: grep -n 'Art\. 3(2)|extraterritorial|targets.*EU|EU representative|Art\. 27' app lib _docs _rules _backend-system returns nothing.
findings.existing_coverage: partial: the policy correctly hedges with 'ggf.' rather than flatly asserting GDPR applies; it never resolves the hedge
findings.where_it_should_live: _backend-system/research/privacy-data-protection.md (the scoping determination, one paragraph) + the privacy policy's section 7 wording once decided
findings.enforcement: checklist; a legal-scoping decision, not a gate
